But we have had our difficulties in the past in establishing manufacturing industries in this country. Those' difficulties have been largely overcome, and it would appear to me that the manufacturers of eastern Canada might very well concede that the requests of the western Canadian farmers were not by any means premature ; and, while the reductions on these manufactured articles are not as great as we might hope to see, yet we are glad that the government took those views into consideration, and made substantial reductions on many important lines of agricultural implements.
Now, Sir, I have just one word more to say on this question : So far as I have been able to ascertain the sentiment of the people of wejtern Canada since the announcement of'this trade agreement was made, has been one of entire approval of the agreement. We are an optimistic people in western Canada. There may be those in eastern Canada who conceive that their interests have been injured by this agreement; and I am free to say that the large deputation that visited this chamber some days ago for the purpose of interviewing the government with respect to the apprehended injury which it would bring to the fruit-growing industry of Canada, had a large measure of my sympathy. But I cannot see for the life of me wherein the contention of that deputation can possibly be true when they come to prove the agreement after it is put into effect. If our soil and climate are adapted to fruit growing, I cannot see why the Canadian fruitgrower cannot compete with the fruity growers of any other country. So far as the home markets are concerned, they have the benefit of a less cost for transportation. If there be anything in the argument that fruit is grown cheaper in the southern states because of the cheapness of coloured labour, that surely is made up for by the lesser cost of transportation from our

orchards to our home markets; and I am satisfied that the opinion expressed by many fruit-growers in the Niagara peninsula and in other fruit districts of Ontario, that the best thing that has ever happened to our fruit industry has been the placing of fruit on the free list, will eventually prove to be a true prophecy.
There was one other point in the argument advanced by the hon. member tor North Toronto which I think is worthy of a moment's consideration. He said that if this agreement went through, it would tend to discourage the investment of foreign capital in Canadian enterprise and Canadian securities. Well, Sir, I wonder what is the consideration that attracts the British or other capitalist when he comes to invest his money. Is it a question of what flag the country flies, or is it a question of what interest he can get on his money? I think that is the answer to the hon. gentleman's argument. To my mind, instead of capital being frightened away from investment in Canadian industries and Canadian securities as a result of this *agreement, there will be such rapid development and prosperity in this country that we shall find an ever-increasing stream of population coming from other countries, bringing with it more and more capital for investment in this country and for the development of our national enterprises.
Sir, I have only to say in conclusion that while conscious of my inability to do justice to the many important features of this agreement, I believe that, if it is ratified by this parliament and by the Congress of the United States, as we have every reason to believe it will be, it will prove to be a measure of the greatest possible relief to the producers and the consumers of both these great countries; and the public man who undertakes to stand in the way of an arrangement which opens up the markets to the south of us for the product of our Canadian farms, so that the tillers [DOT]of the soil in this country will get the opportunity for which they have been longing for _years, will assume a most serious responsibility, and one for which sooner or later he will have to give an account at the bar of public opinion.

There is another great aspect of this question besides the purely Canadian one to which I have not referred, and which to thoughtful people presents great dangers and gives cause for much anxiety. I allude to the diversion of trade from that great country which is the mother of our free institutions and the source and inspiration of much that is best in our national life. With Great Britain and with other British dominions across the seas it is the earnest wish of the Canadian people to form closer ties, commercial and other. It may be true that Britain has been slow to take what some may conceive to have been the necessary steps, it may be true that Australia has regrettably delayed in her efforts to foster closer commercial ties with this country; but at least this government may well have waited to discuss these high matters at the imperial conference next May. The .Prime Minister knew well that such matters would be discussed; knew that it was the earnest desire of all the dominions to strengthen the bonds commercial and national between our scattered peoples. Why could he not, in fairness, wait before plunging the country into a step which makes, not for unity, but for disintegration in the empire. We were doing well enough -the hour had struck for the republic to the south to move in new directions-it had not struck for us. This, too, will be counted heavily against the men who to-day are assuming to guide us into paths when'the instructions for so guiding us have not been given to them. Government speakers deride the suggestion that there is any national danger in the drift and final tendency of this new policy. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) in a speech which was characterised by time-worn platitudes and many extraordinary omissions, closed by regretting that there was any opposition to this proposal. He added: ' I regret it for the sake of hon. gentlemen opposite.' Sir, is the minister fatuous enough, misguided enough, to dream that British Columbia members can fall down and worship the golden calf he has set up?
Mining is one of our foremost interests, and the particular section of that enormous industry which might have been helped by free, or easier entry of its ores into the United States is the zinc industry. Did the minister lift a hand to help it in this way? Not he. This is something for the Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman) to explain to the people of his province. Did the Minister of Customs, after dealing a knock-out blow to the fruit industry of British Columbia expect us not to oppose this measure? Sir, all through his speech there was not a single word which even acknowledged the existence of the fruit in-Mr. BURRELL.
dustry. Whether he was ashamed to touch it, or afraid to, I cannot say. And then, Sir, the Minister of Customs closes by saying:
Well, I am sorry to say they appear unwilling to join in this last patriotic movement for the benefit of the people of this country.
We do not join because we do not believe that it makes for the permanent benefit of this country. We do not join because we believe it is not patriotic, that in the last analysis it will be found to undermine and destroy Canadian and imperial patriotism. Thoughtful men on both sides of the water are to-day feeling this. Prominent statesmen in Great Britain have voiced their fears. And, Sir, what did this government immediately do? The Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) sent a cablegram to Lord Stratheona, and conveyed the impression that Canada was, or ought to be, a unit in the matter. His precise wrords were:	[DOT]
It is evident that some British journalists and public men have received erroneous impressions concerning the reciprocity agreement. Reciprocal trade relations with the United States have been the policy of all parties in Canada for generations.
Sir, I may not very well understand political ethics, but this is a strange message to place before the people of Great Britain. If the end justifies the means, if all is fair in political war, there is nothing to say. But there are many people in Canada who will condemn so singular a use of official power as this. The policy of all parties in Canada for generations!-I need not labour this point, "in the powerful speech which has been delivered by the member for North Toronto he has dealt with this whole matter in a way which will make a tremendous appeal to the thinking men of this country. So far from the Conservative party being tied up to this policy we have long cut loose from it. The trend of events in Canada for the past score of years has been in otheT directions. Years ago Mr. James G. Blaine said ' We will give you reciprocity if you will discriminate against Great Britain in our favour.' We know that when that famous proposition of commercial union was made by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in 1891, he was unable even to retain within his party Mr. Blake who saw then, as he would see now, whither such a step would lead. Let me give the Prime Minister a few extracts from Mr. Blake's letters which are singularly applicable to the present hour. Speaking of commercial union he said:
No manufacturer, looking to the continental market, would fix or even enlarge his capital or business in the country of five millions at the risk of being cut off from the country of sixty-five millions. Our neighbours, instead of engaging in manufactures here, would

take our markets with goods manufactured there. And our raw material, instead of being finished on the ground, would be exported to be finished abroad. Uncertainty would alarm capital and paralyze enterprise.
Could there be any statements more absolutely apropos to the present proposals before the House? But Mr. Blake went further, and sounded a note of alarm which the people of this country should heed at the present hour:
Assuming that absolute free trade with the States thus described as commercial union, may and ought to come, I believe that it can and should come only as an incident, or at any rate, as a well understood precursor of political union, for which indeed we should be able to make better terms before than after the surrender of our commercial independence.
Now those were the words of a man whose intellectual force carried enormous weight in this country, and he would have nothing of such a proposition. The proposals now before the House are leading in the same fatal direction as they led in 1891. The advocates of reciprocity on the other side of the line are speaking of annexation as a logical result. Let me point out what President Taft said the other day in speaking to the Illinois legislature :
It will give to the United States much greater control of the wheat market than it ever had before. It will enable its milling plants to turn Canadian wheat into flour and send abroad its finished product, and it will stimulate the sale of manufactures and-other things that we have to sell to Canada.
Chairman McCall, of the Ways and Means Committee, in his report, says significantly:
And the benefit to us would be enormous if we could sweep away all tariffs between the two countries, it would have the effect upon our trade of another Louisiana purchase.
And still more significant is the closing paragraph of his report:
The Bill takes a long step towards establishing for the continent of North America a policy of unrestricted trade and eommerec. 1
If that is not commercial union, what is the meaning of the English language? Now there are other proofs of the certainty with which hve are drifting along this road. Senator Beveridge, one of the ardent and able expounders of reciprocity, said the other day:
There must be reciprocity with Canada. Our tariff with the rest of the world does not apply to our northern neighbour. That policy already has driven American manufacturers to cross the Canadian borders, build vast plants with American capital on Canadian soil, employing Canadian workingmen to supply trade. That capital should be kept at
home to employ American workingmen to supply Canadian demands.

Hearst says:
Let us have commercial union first, and political union afterwards.	.
Now surely no man can avoid seeing where the Canadian people are drifting in this matter. Canada is literally to be the hewer of wood, the drawer of water, the purveyor of food to the powerful nation which aims by such an arrangement to be the great workshop of the continent. The Prime Minister, willing to go one step, will soon be willing, or be forced, to take the other. Great as is his facility for swallowing his own words, he can hardly forget the passion with which, on the platforms of this country in 1896, he vowed that he would not be satisfied until he had wiped out every vestige of protection.-Sir, it is in vain that the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) thunders forth about the patriotism and the benefits of this measure. In the long run it will be neither patriotic nor beneficial, but subversive of both.
Now it was not my intention so much to indicate the national dangers in connection with these proposals, as to point out to the House and the country, one dark blot in particular on the pages of this agreement, and to protest in the most vigorous manner possible against a grievous wrong that is being done to a great national industry, the fruit industry of Canada. What has been the animating principle governing my hon. friends the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance in making their arrangements with the negotiators at Washington? Certainly the desire, the oft confessed and repeated desire, on their part to find for the producer of Canada a freer and a wider market. I noticed that when the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) was speaking just now, he practically agreed to the soundness of this argument. I took down his words:
' The agricultural classes are the foundation of this country '. Well, we can all

agree to that, and I presume he will include the fruit growers of this country as forming part of the agriculturists. He touched on the very small reduction in the duty on agricultural implements, but he thought it was helpful, and added: ' The farmers are reasonable people, they do not expect a revolution ', that is, they do not expect to sweep away protective duties. ' They are satisfied for the present to get free markets for their products '. That was his argument, and it was the argument that had all along been put forward by the government. Let me remark to my hon. friend that although he did not believe in the revolutionary process of sweeping away the duties on agricultural implements, the government is now proposing to sweep away the duties on the fruit industry, and my hon. friend does not object. hope, as one who has warm sympathy for the coal trade, that they will be able to stand it \ Turn to his remarks about the trifling reduction of duties on agricultural implements, a reduction so small as to little affect either consumer or producer. I quote the whole passage and ask the House to note the extraordinary significance of the words and their logical application to the case of the fruit-growing industry of Canada:
With regard to agricultural implements, the House need not be reminded of the strong desire on the part of our western farmers to have better terms on these articles. They would be glad to have them free of duty, but anxious as I am to meet their views I must frankly say to them that we do not think that is fair. Like all others they must be( prepared to give and take, they must bel prepared to bear their share in the burdens of the country, and I believe that when the matter is fairly put to the farmers, they will recognize that principle. We do not propose to make agricultural implements free but to make some reductions, and we trust that, while these may not be all the farmers want, they will be evidence of the desire of the government to meet their views as far as possible without doing any injustice to the industries of Canada.
Without doing any injustice to the industries of Canada? Mr. Chairman, in wiping off every vestige of protection which the Canadian producer of fruit has hitherto been afforded, the minister has violated the very principles laid down by himself. He has singled out one large class of pro-Mr. BURRELL
ducers, and one only, and has dealt that great industry a blow, the effect of which, will be a shrinkage in value of all the great orchard areas of Canada and especially of Ontario and British Columbia, and the discouragement of thousands who have invested their all in slowly building up what has come to be recognized as one of our great national assets.	*
Mr. Chairman, I shall make no apology for dealing with this matter with some degree of fulness. I am persuaded that few men in this House appreciate the nature of the blow which has been struck. I am equally persuaded that members ,of this House will recognize the injustice of the blow, when they are more fully apprised of the facts. I may not know any more or as much of political economy as many of my hon. friends opposite, but they will admit that 28 consecutive years spent in the practical work of fruit growing ought at least to enable a man to speak with some little authority as to what will help, or what will hurt, the special business in which he has been so long engaged. I have stated that the case of the fruit-growers stands out as a glaring instance of one large body of producers who are unquestionably going to be injuriously affected by this arrangement. The government's own action in the past warrants the statement. In 1896 the House will remember that great uneasiness was manifested as to the trade policy of the present government. The country had been led to believe that widespread reductions of the tariff would follow and the rapidly growing fruit industry shared the general alarm. It fell to my lot to assist in the preparation and presentation of the fruit-growers' case to the Tariff Commissioners, who were the very ministers who have negotiated the present reciprocal arrangement with the United States. In the course of my remarks, I shall have to summarize the arguments and data then put forward, but I may simply state now that the commissioners were sufficiently impressed with the strength of the fruit-growers' case to decide that the moderate protection they then had, should be continued. Under that decision, the industry still further expanded. Since that time we have witnessed the establishment of commercial horticulture in my own province of British Columbia, and the investment of enormous capital in all lines of horticultural development. In 1905-6 the government undertook an exhaustive investigation of tariff matters and for that purpose a commission toured the country from ocean to ocean, giving careful hearing to all Canadian industries. Again it fell to my lot to assist in presenting the case of the fruit-growers to the commissioners, this time in British Columbia, and still to the same two ministers, the Min-

ister of Finance, and Minister of Customs. Strong as the case was, and is, for Ontario it was still stronger for the far west, and once more, after full consideration, the government acknowledged the justice and strength of our pleas and the industry remained in statu quo. I ask the government, I ask the Minister of Finance, have circumstances altered since that date ? Is the case weakened at the present moment, nay, is it not rather strengthened ? He cannot reply that the wiping out of the United States tariff alters it. Not at any time did we urge this feature. It was not free entry into the States but protection against a mammoth and more favoured competitor in our own markets that we persistently asked for.
When that 'has induced the government to do what an overwhelming majority of the fruit producers of Canada have implored them not to do, and agreed not to do in 1907, Sir, I am driven to the only possible conclusion, viz : that our interests have been bartered away for privileges to other interests which otherwise may have been difficult to obtain. I am justified in such a conclusion, (by a significant passage in President Taft's message to Congress. In the main President Taft has considered the interests of the American consumer but in fruit no one knows better than he that the American consumer will receive no benefit and he frankly and directly acknowledges that he has taken this step in the interests of the American producer. He says : It has (been found possible to obtain free entry into -Canada for -fresh Truits and-vegetables-a matter of special value to the south and to the Pacific coast in disposing of their products in their -season.' Here tnen is *the United States reason, nakedly, plainly expressed for reciprocal free trade in fruit. What answer has this government got? What justification can it offer to the House, to the country, and to the industry itself for thus penalizing the Canadian grower in his -already difficult fight against an immensely powerful foreign competitor in the Canadian market. Absolutely none 1 Sir, this industry means far more to Canada than the layman realizes. It means so much that anything which can in the slightest degree injuriously affect it is an injury to the -whole of Canada. W'hat has been our continual pride and boa-st in -Canada tout this, that we are a nation, not primarily of shopkeepers, but of farmers. The settlement of every great province of the Dominion has been the history of settlement of the land, the foundation of the rural homes, from which have sprung so much that is strong and clean in our national life. We have arrived now at a different stage. The problem, acute in all older countries, is -already showing itself here, that of too -great a congestion of the cities and towns, 'mere is a vital reason
for the universal cry ' back to the land,' and in no form is that cry so successful as when it appeals to the -man to throw his energies into horticultural work. The first effort of the new settler to create a real home in his new environment was the planting of the orchard. The man who plants 'trees thereby gives hostages to that particular spot of earth. Unlike the cattle man, the sheep man, the general agriculturist, he is in no sense nomadic. Consciously or unconsciously he has pledged himself to his soil. Each additional tree planted ties him more firmly to his home. In the earlier days it- was not without doubts that he did plant. Canada was reputed the great north land of snow, ice, and harsh climate. Those pioneers who had courage and faith to attempt the beginning of our orchard work builded better than they knew, and deserve the heartfelt -gratitude of those who came later. With the progress of years, with the growing proofs, orchard work branched out into a special industry, and thirty years ago, though as compared with the present development still small, it bad assumed in various portions of Ontario and eastern Canada a large importance. It called for a heavier investment than ordinary agriculture. It demanded a more special attention, and I may here fitly quote the words of Dr. James Robertson that :
The highest form of labour applied to the cultivation of the soil is that of the horticulturist.
___It_. involved years, -not only of patient
labour but of patient wuuHngjMor financial results, and in all these things it deserved and will ever deserve, the -sympathy of the great mass of Canadians who are following other pursuits. In 1890 to tire Montreal Horticultural Society was entrusted the task of organizing the first conference of fruit growers throughout the Dominion- the seal and sign of the industry having attained something like a national growth. Expansion continued and when the census of 1901 was taken we have the following figures of development : Apple trees, 15,053,875 ; peach trees, 1,301,775, -pear trees, 962,101 ; plums, 2,415,695 ; cherry, 1,288,368 ; other fruit trees, 179,425. A total of over t-wenty-one million trees besides 2,783,596 grape vines, and large acreages of small fruits.
In 'this large area amounting to nearly
400,000	acres of orchard the great province of Ontario ranked first with nearly seventy per cent of the total, Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island following, in the order -named. It is impossible to state accurately the increase in the last ten years but from the careful researches which I have made I am -approximately correct when I place the -present acreage at more

than half a million acres. The most remarkable growth is in British Columbia where since the census we have increased ten times, having at the present time some
5,000,000 trees representing roughly from
100,000	to 110,000 acres.
Does the government ; do members of this House realize what these figures mean; what potential and actual wealth of investment they represent? Ten acres of bearing orchards will supply the railroads with freight equivalent to that from 100 acres of grain. Ten acres of orchard means the employment of practically as much labour as that employed in 100 acres of wheat land. A similar proportion exists in reference to values and I am giving, the House a very conservative estimate indeed When I place the orchards of the Dominion of Canada at a valuation of $150,000,000. But if these figures imply an industry so important as to deserve the amplest consideration at the hands of the government, I ought to also point out other equally strong reasons for the same consideration. The great bulk of these 30,000,000 trees are apples. The development of these orchards calls for special skill, and great expenditures, and a close and eternal vigilance against innumerable enemies of the orch-ardist. It means five or six years in the west, and eight or ten years in the east, 'before the fruit-grower gets returns which will even pay current expenses, and many more years before he can hope to be recouped for his years of constructive but not productive work. In this respect his position is more nearly similar to the manufacturer, who is through a series of years perfecting his plant and machinery before he makes his large output. He is in a more hazardous and difficult position than the ordinary farmer. The wheat grower, the cattle grower can under pressure of adverse circumstances move to fresh fields and pastures new. The orchardist must stand or fall by the capital which he has locked up in the trees which have taken many years of patient intelligent toil to bring to the stage of production, and any blow which strikes him must strike with exceptional severity, and it can be demonstrated beyond a shadow of a doubt that such a blow will be dealt if the proposals now before the House go through.
I have referred to the fruit-growing industry as a great national asset. It is in very truth such an asset. No specialized form of agricultural industry employs an equally large amount of labour with corresponding distribution of wages. It adds a heavy volume of traffic to the railways of the country. It feeds large and import-and subsidiary interests such as box barrel and basket manufactories, canneries, nurseries, cold storage plants, and so on. It does an invaluable service to the country by building up compact and thickly-Mr. BURRELL.
settled communities of the best type and it affords to the world the best proof of the unrivalled climate and soil of the country. It was not long since we laboured under the imputation of being ' Our Lady of the Snows/ and you need not go far in the world even now to find the idea prevalent that this great land of the north is an inhospitable clime. There is no finer or more convincing proof to the sceptic to the contrary than that which is afforded by the magnificent fruit grown in Canadian orchards and coloured by Canadian sunshine. Sir, I remember in 1884 the first visit of the British Association to this country. Some of the world's influential men were in that great group of men, many of whom, for the first time, set foot on our soil. They, too, had harsh and convinced ideas of the character of the country. I can recall a number of them standing on the wharf at the old town of Niagara-on-the-Lake when 10,000 baskets of peaches were awaiting shipment to Toronto. It was a revelation to them, and thousands of dollars of government literature could not have conveyed the truth to those men in the manner which that sight did. Yet, of all the branches of the industry, peach-culture will be hit the hardest if reciprocal free trade in fruit becomes an accomplished fact. The theory set forth by the government, is that free entry of our fruit into the United States will compensate for such losses as we may sustain by the unrestricted influx of American fruit. I am not dealing with anything but the effect on the producer. I will touch the case of the consumer later. I have been at some pains to obtain information from authoritative sources as to the effect of these proposals in the east. Those near the border believe that the sale of their earlier apples and berries will be helped by free entry to New England markets, and I am not disputing it, although I may here point out that New England annually produces 3,000,000 barrels of apples, of which she exports twenty per cent, so that too much faith cannot be pinned to that market for apples. Nova Scotia, by far the most important horticultural area in the east, is essentially an apple-producing province, and ships, and will always ship, the great bulk of her crop to England. Prior to 1907 her exports for several years averaged 400,000 barrels. In 1909, 700,000 barrels were exported. Last year was a comparative failure.
A somewhat small percentage, then, of the whole industry in the east will be helped by these proposals. On the other hand, there will be no great effect one way or the other on the main industry. I may quote a telegram, which I have received from Mr. S. C. Parker, of Berwick, Nova Scotia, one of the foremost authorities in

the maritime provinces, and the weight ol whose name was used by the Prime Minister on behalf of free fruit, in his reply to the delegation which came here the other day. His telegram to me was as follows:
Nova Scotia fruit growers practically indifferent to abolition of fruit duty. Britain is our market for winter apples. For early apples think we will gain on United States. Berry growers are pleased.
It must be borne in mind, however, that important as the fruit industry is to the maritime provinces-and fruit-growers elsewhere in the Dominion will rejoice in their progress-it occupies relatively a small position in respect to the whole industry-in the Dominion. Quebec is not producing for export to any extent, and it is absolutely sure that New York State with its immense production will with free fruit find a favourable market in Quebec, and this will not tend to increase the price of his product to the Quebec grower. I am informed by good authorities that, outside of cranberries and wild berries, the orchard acreage in New Brunswick is approximately 10,000 acres. I am informed by an equally good authority that in Nova Scotia it would approximate 25,000 acres. I am aware that great progress in planting has been made in recent years, and a fair estimate for all kinds of cultivated fruits in the Dominion would be as follows:

Admittedly their chief market is England, and it will at once be seen that the benefits from free fruit, if benefits there are, affect only a very small portion of the industry in the east, while the enormous and valuable orchards of British Columbia are badly smitten, to say nothing of Ontario.
Now as to Ontario, fruit-growing is scattered over a wide portion of the province, but for climatic reasons necessarily centred more heavily in certain districts. Lincoln, with 20,169 acres of fruit heads the list of the great fruit counties of the' province. There follow in order of importance Northumberland, Middlesex, Grey, Wentworth, Huron, Kent, Prince Edward county, Lambton, Simcoe, Norfolk, Essex, Hastings, Oxford and York, besides many others ranking closely behind. The great bulk of this fruit, more especially the more tender classes, is marketed in the Canadian
markets of the east. A considerable portion, especially of apples, finds its way across the ocean, an increasing quantity reaches the markets of the prairies, and a small percentage across the international boundary. The United States fruit-grower then sends into the markets of this country, under present conditions, from five to six times the amount that the Canadian grower sends into his markets. What will be the effect of the abolition of the duties? Undoubtedly a lessening of the producer's prices in these markets. The reasons for such a statement are obvious to those who have given this matter any study and are perfectly plain to those great fruit-producing states who have, in their own interests, been instrumental in getting fruit placed on the free list.
It may be remarked that while the Canadian duty on apples is less than that imposed by the United States on apples entering their country, yet with other fruits it is not so. In the case of pears and plums the duties are nearly the same, the Canadian tariff being a shade higher. Grapes come here facing a duty of 2c per lb., while our product would face a duty of 25c per cubic foot, or less than the Canadian tariff. Peaches, with a duty of twenty-five cents a bushel in the United States, face a duty nearly twice as high on entering this country. Berries, on which the ' Canadian grower has now a protection of

2c per lb., enter the United States with a duty of only lc per quart. Yet, in spite of having to face a higher tariff to get into this market, the United States grower, in 1910, placed $210,796 worth of berries into this market, or practically equivalent to all the fruit shipped into the United States from this country, with the exception of apples.
Let us take for a moment the case of grapes. In 1883, when I first became connected with grape culture in Ontario, we obtained 10c per lb. for the fruit. Year by year, with added acreage, increased output and strong competition amongst the Canadian growers, the price came steadily down, until the Canadian consumer could obtain the fruit at a price which put it within the reach of all, and left an extremely small profit for the grower. For the past eight or ten years the average wholesale price to the grower would Tun, for his main crop, from a cent to a cent and a half per pound. The ordinary commercial package is the eight-pound basket. For this he obtains from 12 to 15 cents. But, Sir, the late Mr. Murray Pettit, one of the foremost and ablest of those who cultivated this fruit on a large scale, estimated that grapes cost 12c per basket to produce. It is, therefore, obvious that the grower's main opportunity for getting a fair profit for the whole crop lies in the special cultivation of earlier varieties, when the price is somewhat higher. The Canadian grower can and does produce enough to amply satisfy the needs of the Canadian consumer, and the present duty of 2c per lb. simply secures some immunity to the grower here against a wholesale and disastrous exploitation of his own market by New York state, which has more than 6Cb-
000	acres of grapes under cultivation. These things were very ably put before the government, in the tariff discussion of 1907, by Mr. E. D. Smith, then member for Wentworth, and then, as now, an acknowledged authority on the subject. Right here I will call the attention of the Minister of Customs to a remark made by him in that very discussion. It will be found on page 1914 of ' Hansard,' 1907. The minister says, in answering Mr. Smith:
I have listened to the hon. gentleman's remarks in regard to grapes. If I might state my own personal views I think there is a great deal in what he says, hut I am of the opinion that his remarks which would apply with force to grapes, would not apply with equal force to peaches. In reference to grapes
1	think he is right.
Let me ask the minister how he can reconcile his words and conviction then with his attitude now. His answer then was directly applied to the argument that United States competition would ilnjure the Canadian grower. Four years have passed. The conditions have not changed, Mr. BURRELL.
or if they have only in a direction which makes the case still stronger for the Canadian grower. In the face of the minister's strongly worded belief at that time, I can only again assume, and I am amply justified in doing so, that he and his colleague have sacrificed our industry and their own convictions in order to benefit some one else.

speechtext: Was there not a duty on grapes going into the United States at that time?

maintopic: RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I have explained that.

speechtext: It makes all the difference in the world.

speechtext: I do not think the minister's (Mr. Paterson's) remarks are well timed or very relevant. I have already explained that the duty on grapes coming into this country is greater than the duty on grapes going into the United States. The hon. minister will not question that. And, with the enormous acreage of New York state, they are able amply to supply their own market, and their enormous output will not permit of us getting into that market with any profit; but the removal of the duty will assist the growers there, at certain seasons when prices are somewhat higher, to crowd into our market.

maintopic: RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I am only pointing out that, if the hon. gentleman wishes to be fair, he must recognize the difference in the conditions. At that time there was a duty against our fruit going into the United States; under this agreement there will be no such duty. When the fruit growers and others who spoke on this question addressed the tariff commission, tbe argument they used was that the United States duties were much higher against us than ours against them-I am not alluding to the particular item of grapes, but am speaking of the general argument,'-and they ask that our duty be put up to equal theirs so that we might be on fair and equal terms. The terms will be fair and equal, so far as tariff is concerned, under this Bill.

maintopic: RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I am afraid the minister has not followed the course of my remarks very closely. He evidently has not followed what I stated with reference to that very tariff commission.

I think not. I am speaking about all the conditions of growth and

crops and not the conditions of tariff. 1 know that the conditions of tariff under these proposals are different, but I am speaking of the condition of the crop, of production and the result of the producer's investment. As to what the minister has said, I followed all these tariff proposals.
He knows well that I helped put upi the case for British Columbia; he knows that I did the same for Ontario in 1896. I could bring resolution after resolution to prove that his statement is not correct- that it is only a half truth. It is true that the growers of Canada have always said that the United States tariff is much greater than ours and that ours should be raised to equal theirs. But he will not find in one resolution in a hundred-not one in a thousand-anything to show that any association or grower believed that it *would be a benefit to have the duty *entirely taken off. We never argued -and the minister himself knew it-that the abolition of these duties would put us on fair terms. It would put us on equal terms in one sense, but on hopelessly unequal terms in another1 sense. The minister ought to know that. And I think that if he will permit me to continue my argument I will drive this fact home with compelling force, if he is willing to listen to a fair statement of the case. The minister ought to admit, if he knows anything of my general method of argument in this House, that I try to avoid putting up an unfair argument. I want to put my case fairly, even in those matters which tell against myself. I am so deeply interested in this industry and my convictions are so profound that this is a serious blow, and that that fact can be so clearly proven, that I want to be perfectly fair in my contentions.

maintopic: RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burrell) a question? Do not the grapes come in much earlier in the United States than in Canada?

maintopic: RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Certainly. I am going to cover all these arguments as I go off. I had dealt with the question of grapes and when the minister interrupted me I was about to take up the subject of peaches. Now, as to peaches:	In 1907 in the tariff
discussion to which I have alluded, Mr. E.	D. Smith, then member for Wentworth, was asking for a duty of 3 cents per pound. The minister (Mr. Paterson) refused, but he was satisfied that 2 cents the present duty-was fair. The peach industry is not only a very large industry in Ontario, but an important one in my own province,, and in a variety of ways is one which deserves the special sympathy and encouragement of Canada generally. The area of peach culture in Canada, owing to peculiarly favourable requirements of soil and climate is comparatively limited. It takes some
years of waiting before the productive stage is reached. The crops are not always regular, danger from frosts is always present, the investment in the industry is heavy. Not always do the growers reap a reward commensurate with the labour and investment. I remember vividly the last large crop we had before I left Ontario. I think it was in 1897. The crop matured quickly, markets were flooded, and in common with many others I had thousands of baskets on which I got absolutely no return, not even sufficient to pay the cost of production. Those people who attempt to argue that free competition from the United States will not injure the producer in Canada are absolutely ignorant of the facts. Sir, facing a duty now of twice their own the American grower sent into this country last year 200 carloads valued at $155,000. What he will do when that cent a pound is removed is easily foreseen. It must be borne in mind that the great southern states have immense areas adapted for successful peach culture. The crop can be cultivated by cheap labour and handled as it is on an enormous scale with every facility of transportation they are in a position of great advantage compared to . our own. But it is not only the southern states, i Through Delaware, Maryland and northerly to Michigan and New York the areas still exist. I am leaving out the Pacific coast phase for the moment. I am in close touch with friends in New York state who are intimately connected with horticultural work and what is their frank opinion as to
-all-This._Sir, they tell me that they are de-
'lighted at the prospect onfeeTfuit; that~ western New York will find an easy and profitable market now in the cities of Ontario and Quebec, and while candidly admitting that it will be a hard blow on the Canadian grower they are very cheerful as to their own benefits. The more thoroughly one looks into this question the more one is amazed that ministers of the Crown, who were presumably guarding, or should have guarded the interests of the Canadian fruit farmer, have thus injured and discouraged him.
Before leaving the case of the Canadian producer in the east, a case which becomes stronger the more closely it is examined, I desire to point out in passing the nature of the injury which will be inflicted on the vegetable growers of the country. In Ontario no less than 57,000 acres are given up to market gardening and vegetable growing. In my own province we are to-day shipping hundreds of carloads of vegetables, practically none of which go to the other side of the line, but which do meet a ^ heavy competition from the states of Washington and Oregon. The government has had laid before it in detail the case of this class of producer. It is intensive farm-

ing in a very real sense. It involves an immense expenditure in labour, a heavy investment of capital and a large portion of this investment depends altogether for its return on the prices obtained in our cities and towns in the early part of the season. Wipe out such protection as they now have and you expose these men with their millions of investment to a fierce competition from the tremendous area devoted to this class of work in the United States. An earlier season, a vast area, low priced labour, are the factors which will enable the American producer to filch such small profits as he now has from the home grower.
Sir, arguments of this character are not advanced solely from this side of the House. Two years ago the pi'esent member for Wentworth (Mr. Sealey) a supporter of this government through thick and thin, moved a resolution asking for greater protection to the fruit and vegetable growers and argued at great length that the present duties on fruit and vegetables were not sufficient and that this * government ought to increase them, and see that Canadian growers were not crowded out of their own market. What will that hon. member do now that his government has given free entrance to United States produce thereby dealing a smashing blow to my hon. friend's constituents?
Now, before leaving the case of Ontario, I want to refer particularly to the demands made by that great delegation of 800 fruit growers from Ontario generally, and from the Niagara district in particular, and to the Prime Minister's answer. I have a good deal more to say, and if the Prime Minister would allow me to move the adjournment of the debate, I would esteem it a favour.
